title: The Babylonian Talmud
hookLine: the academies' long conversation is gathered and sealed into the Talmud studied today

cards: Where is the teacher standing? That is the first question of the Babylonian Talmud. It copies out the Mishnah's opening line, the one we read this week: from when may the Shema be said in the evening?
And before answering, it pushes back. Who said there is any duty at all? Where does this come from?

Then it answers itself with a verse of the Torah, which in the 1917 Jewish translation says to speak of these things "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." The Mishnah opened with a question.
The Talmud opens with a question about the question.

teach.b: The Babylonian Talmud, the Bavli, is the record of the academies we met yesterday: generation after generation of Babylonian sages questioning the Mishnah, line by line.
It's mostly in Aramaic, the everyday language of those rooms, with the Mishnah's Hebrew quoted piece by piece. It argues. It tells stories.
It wanders into dreams, medicine and the rain, then comes back to the law.
Like the Mishnah, it keeps views that did not win, with names attached; even its first page gives two answers to one question and keeps both. Then the book was closed.

teach.h: RAV ASHI AND RAVINA: THE END.
teach.b: The Talmud names the moment in one brief sentence: Rav Ashi and Ravina are the end of instruction. Tradition reads that as the sealing. Later teachers would explain and rule, but they would not add to the Talmud.
Sealed doesn't mean finished with. It means a fixed text, so that everyone after could open the same page and argue about it together. Now step back over this week.
Akiva saying the Shema with his last breath. Eleh ezkerah. Nasi writing it down.
The Mishnah. The Talmud of the land. The academies by the rivers.

teach.h: A BOOK YOU CAN CARRY ANYWHERE.
teach.b: And now the Bavli: a people losing its Temple and its land, and building a book you can carry anywhere.

how: Jews study the Babylonian Talmud in yeshivas and study halls, often in pairs called chavruta, and some follow Daf Yomi, a cycle of one page a day.

the Talmud names its own ending

it asks right away where the duty comes from, and why evening comes before morning.

games.q: you're a student in the academy. the Mishnah speaks of the evening Shema before the morning one. a friend asks why evening comes first. what do you say?
o: the Torah's own order: lying down before rising up, and evening before morning.
games.why: the Talmud gives two answers and keeps both: the verse puts lying down before rising up, and in creation the evening comes before the morning.

practice: On that same first page, the Talmud asks why the Mishnah speaks of evening before morning.
One answer is the verse itself, which puts lying down before rising up; the other reaches back to creation, where, in the 1917 Jewish translation, "there was evening and there was morning, one day."

Evening first: in this reading, a day begins as the light goes, with rest, so breathe slowly and think of this evening as the start of tomorrow. If you pray, you can give thanks, in words you know, for the day that is ending.

wordCard.voice: Bavli. The everyday name for the Babylonian Talmud, the academies' long argument over the Mishnah, mostly in Aramaic, closed with Rav Ashi and Ravina.

orig.note: Hebrew: the Babylonian Talmud, often just called the Bavli.

carryVoice: Your line: the talmud sealed. A fixed page, and an argument that never closed. Day nine hundred ten, and the week is whole.
